content: Progressive lung damage is the leading cause of mortality in individuals with cystic fibrosis. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, have been proposed as a potential therapeutic option to prevent the progressive decline in pulmonary function and associated morbidity in this population. This review represents an update of previously published findings. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy of oral NSAID therapy in individuals with cystic fibrosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, which includes references from electronic databases, hand-searched journals, and conference abstracts. Additionally, manufacturers of NSAIDs were contacted, and online trial registries were reviewed. The most recent search of the Trials Register was performed on November 21, 2018. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared oral NSAIDs, administered at any dose for a minimum of two months, to placebo in individuals with cystic fibrosis. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion and evaluated their risk of bias. The quality of evidence for each outcome was rated using the GRADE guidelines. The search identified 17 trials, of which four met the inclusion criteria, encompassing a total of 287 participants aged between 5 and 39 years, with a maximum follow-up duration of four years. One additional trial is awaiting classification pending the publication of its full report, and two trials are ongoing. Among the included trials, three compared ibuprofen to placebo (two of which were conducted at the same center and included overlapping participants), while one trial evaluated piroxicam versus placebo. The three ibuprofen trials were determined to have good or adequate methodological quality, although they utilized different outcome measures and summary statistics. The outcomes assessed included lung function, nutritional status, radiological evidence of pulmonary involvement, intravenous antibiotic use, hospital admissions, survival, and adverse effects. Combined data from the two largest ibuprofen trials demonstrated a slower annual decline in lung function, as measured by the percentage of predicted forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1). The mean difference (MD) was 1.32% (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.21 to 2.42), with moderate-quality evidence. Similarly, forced vital capacity (FVC) showed a mean difference of 1.27% (95% CI 0.26 to 2.28), and forced expiratory flow at 25%-75% of vital capacity (FEF25%-75%) had a mean difference of 1.80% (95% CI 0.15 to 3.45). A post hoc analysis of data from two trials, stratified by age, revealed that younger children in the ibuprofen group experienced a slower annual decline in FEV1% predicted (MD 1.41%, 95% CI 0.03 to 2.80) and FVC (MD 1.32%, 95% CI 0.04 to 2.60), both supported by moderate-quality evidence. Data from four trials suggested that the proportion of participants with at least one hospitalization might be slightly lower in the ibuprofen group compared to placebo, with a Peto odds ratio of 0.61 (95% CI 0.37 to 1.01), also supported by moderate-quality evidence. In one trial, long-term use of high-dose ibuprofen was associated with reduced intravenous antibiotic use, as well as improvements in nutritional status and radiological evidence of pulmonary health. No major adverse effects were reported in the included trials; however, the statistical power of these studies to detect clinically significant differences in adverse event rates was low. The trial comparing piroxicam to placebo did not raise concerns regarding risk of bias. However, it did not report sufficient data in a format that could be analyzed for this review. No data were available for the primary outcome of lung function, and the available data for hospital admissions showed no significant difference between the piroxicam and placebo groups. Additionally, no analyzable data were available for other outcomes of interest. In conclusion, high-dose ibuprofen appears to slow the progression of lung disease in individuals with cystic fibrosis, particularly in children. These findings suggest that strategies aimed at modulating lung inflammation may provide clinical benefits for this patient population.
